For a vector space $V$ over $k$, set $V^{\otimes0}=k$ and define the
**tensor algebra**

$$T(V)=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}V^{\otimes n}.$$

After fixing the canonical tensor-product associators, multiplication on
homogeneous pure tensors is concatenation:

$$ (v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_m)(w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n)=v_1\otimes\cdots\otimes v_m\otimes w_1\otimes\cdots\otimes w_n.$$

Extend this bilinearly. Each element has finite degree support, so products are
finite sums. Tensor associativity makes concatenation associative, and
$1\in k=V^{\otimes0}$ is its unit. Thus $T(V)$ is a graded unital associative
$k$-algebra. The degree-one inclusion is denoted $j:V\to T(V)$.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring and let $F$ be a finite free $R$-module
with ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$. Define
$\bigwedge F=T_R(F)/(v\otimes v:v\in F)$, graded by tensor degree; write
$e_I=e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_p}$ for
$I=\{i_1<\cdots<i_p\}$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring and let $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ be a finite list of $R$-modules. Any parenthesized tensor product

$$T=M_1\otimes_R\cdots\otimes_RM_k$$

represents $R$-multilinear maps from $M_1\times\cdots\times M_k$: for every $R$-module $P$, composition with $(m_1,\ldots,m_k)\mapsto m_1\otimes\cdots\otimes m_k$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}_R(T,P)$ to the set of multilinear maps into $P$. Different parenthesizations are connected by the unique isomorphism preserving pure tensors.

For $k=0$, take $T=R$ and identify zero-variable multilinear maps with chosen elements of $P$. For $k=1$, take $T=M_1$.

Left, right and two-sided ideals.

Let $R$ be a ring. An additive subgroup $I\le(R,+)$ is a **left ideal** when
$r i\in I$ for every $r\in R$ and $i\in I$, and a **right ideal** when
$i r\in I$ for every such $r,i$.  A **two-sided ideal**, written
$I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$, is both a left and a right ideal.  In a
commutative ring these three notions agree.

derivations.claim: For each $r\ge1$, the displayed sum is multilinear in $(w_1,\ldots,w_r)$, so [F3] defines a linear map on $V^{\otimes r}$. Together with $\iota_v(1)=0$, these maps define $\delta_v:T_k(V)\to T_k(V)$. On a concatenated pair of pure tensors of degrees $p,q$, the first $p$ deletion terms give $\delta_v(x)y$, while each remaining deletion has the extra sign $(-1)^p$ and gives $(-1)^px\delta_v(y)$. Thus $\delta_v(xy)=\delta_v(x)y+(-1)^p x\delta_v(y)$; bilinearity extends this to homogeneous tensors.
Left multiplication gives $\epsilon_v\epsilon_w+\epsilon_w\epsilon_v=0$: in $\Lambda V$, $(v+w)^2=v^2=w^2=0$, so expansion gives $vw+wv=0$.

Let $S$ be the $k$-linear span of the terms $xj(u)^2y$ for $x,y\in T_k(V)$ and $u\in V$. This span contains all the squares, and multiplying its terms on the left or right only changes $x$ or $y$, so it is a two-sided ideal by [F4]. Every two-sided ideal containing all the squares contains $S$, hence $S=J_{\wedge}$ by [F2]. For $u\in V$, $\delta_v(j(u)j(u))=B(v,u)j(u)-j(u)B(v,u)=0$. If $x$ is homogeneous of degree $p$, then for homogeneous $y$ the derivation rule gives $\delta_v(xj(u)^2y)=\delta_v(x)j(u)^2y+(-1)^px\delta_v(j(u)^2)y+(-1)^{p+2}xj(u)^2\delta_v(y)$. Each outer term lies in $J_{\wedge}$ by [F4], and the middle term is zero. By linearity, $\delta_v(J_{\wedge})\subseteq J_{\wedge}$, so $\delta_v$ descends to $\iota_v$ on $\Lambda V$. Since $J_{\wedge}$ is a two-sided ideal, left multiplication by $j(v)$ also descends to $\epsilon_v$.

On a decomposable wedge, every term of $\iota_v\iota_w+\iota_w\iota_v$ deletes two distinct positions. For fixed $i<j$ and fixed choice of which contraction deletes each factor, deleting position $i$ before $j$ changes the second deletion's sign from $(-1)^{j-1}$ to $(-1)^{j-2}$; the two orders therefore have opposite signs and identical scalar coefficient. Pairing all such terms gives zero. If $r<2$, both compositions vanish.

The contraction formula separates the term deleting the first factor and the terms deleting the remaining factors, giving $\iota_v(w\wedge\omega)=B(v,w)\omega-w\wedge\iota_v(\omega)$ on decomposable $\omega$ and hence on all $\omega$. Thus $\iota_v\epsilon_w+\epsilon_w\iota_v=B(v,w)I$.

Adding the three anticommutator identities yields $c(v)c(w)+c(w)c(v)=(B(v,w)+B(w,v))I=2B(v,w)I$. Taking $w=v$ and cancelling $2$ in $k$ gives $c(v)^2=Q(v)I$. Linearity of $\epsilon_v$ and of the contraction formula in $v$ makes $c:V\to\operatorname{End}_k(\Lambda V)$ linear.

Let $k$ be a field with $\operatorname{char}(k)\ne2$, let $V$ be a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, and let $B:V\times V\to k$ be a symmetric bilinear form, not necessarily nondegenerate. Put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. Write $T_k(V)$ for the tensor algebra and $j:V\to T_k(V)$ for its degree-one inclusion ([[def-tensor-algebra-of-a-vector-space]]). For each $v\in V$, set $r_v=j(v)j(v)-Q(v)1$ and let $J_Q$ be the intersection of all two-sided ideals of $T_k(V)$ containing every $r_v$ ([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]]). This family is nonempty because it contains $T_k(V)$, and its intersection is a two-sided ideal; thus $J_Q$ is the smallest such ideal.

Define the **universal Clifford algebra** with the plus-$Q$ convention by

$$\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q):=T_k(V)/J_Q.$$

The quotient operations are induced from $T_k(V)$; the two-sided ideal condition makes multiplication of cosets well defined. Let $q_Q:T_k(V)\to\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ be the quotient map, put $i_Q=q_Q\circ j$, and write $\bar v=i_Q(v)$. The defining relation is $\bar v^{\,2}=Q(v)1$. In this pair, $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ abbreviates $\mathrm{Cl}^{+}(V,Q)$ after this sign convention has been fixed. No nondegeneracy assumption is imposed.

derivations.claim: By [F4], $A$ has the central unital $k$-algebra structure required by [F1], so $f$ extends uniquely to a unital $k$-algebra homomorphism $\widetilde f:T_k(V)\to A$ with $\widetilde f\circ j=f$.

Since $i_Q=q_Q\circ j$, step 2.1 gives $\bar f\circ i_Q=\widetilde f\circ j=f$. Let $g:\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)\to A$ be any other unital $k$-algebra homomorphism with $g\circ i_Q=f$. Then $g\circ q_Q:T_k(V)\to A$ and $\widetilde f$ are unital algebra extensions of the same map $f$ along $j$, because $(g\circ q_Q)\circ j=g\circ i_Q=f=\widetilde f\circ j$. Uniqueness in [F1] gives $g\circ q_Q=\widetilde f=\bar f\circ q_Q$. Since $q_Q$ is surjective by [F3], $g=\bar f$.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic not $2$, let $V$ be finite-dimensional of dimension $n$, and let $B$ be any symmetric bilinear form on $V$, possibly degenerate; put $Q(v)=B(v,v)$. Fix an ordered basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n$. Then

$$1,\qquad \bar e_{i_1}\cdots\bar e_{i_r}\quad(1\le i_1<\cdots<i_r\le n)$$

is a $k$-basis of $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$, so $\dim_k\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)=2^n$. Give $\mathrm{Cl}(V,Q)$ the word-length filtration $F_{-1}=0$ and, for $m\ge0$, let $F_m$ be the span of products of at most $m$ canonical generators. The natural graded algebra map

Left, right and two-sided ideals.

Let $R$ be a ring. An additive subgroup $I\le(R,+)$ is a **left ideal** when
$r i\in I$ for every $r\in R$ and $i\in I$, and a **right ideal** when
$i r\in I$ for every such $r,i$.  A **two-sided ideal**, written
$I\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}R$, is both a left and a right ideal.  In a
commutative ring these three notions agree.
